description: Per-GPU drill-down beneath Algalon / GPU Utilization Quality. Pick a node and one or more GPUs, then walk the same four layers of utilization quality for those devices: allocated (a job holds it), busy (a kernel is resident), actually computing (warps are executing) and computing efficiently (tensor/FP pipes, memory bandwidth, power against the limit), followed by a memory-bandwidth verdict and the anomaly signals (XID, throttling, NVLink errors, clocks) that explain a GPU falling behind. Use the fleet dashboard to find the node worth looking at; use this one to say why.

links.title: Algalon dashboards
links.tooltip: Drill down into the fleet, queue and node views

panels.description: The reading order and the rules that apply to every panel below. When a value looks wrong, check here first which layer of the question it answers.

options.content:
**GPU utilization alone never decides efficiency.** `DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL` only says a kernel was resident on the device during the sample - one busy SM, a dataloader-starved kernel or an NCCL all-reduce wait all read near 100%.

Pick a node and one or more GPUs, then read top to bottom: **1 Allocated** (does a job hold it?) -> **2 Busy** (is a kernel resident?) -> **3 Actually computing** (are warps executing?) -> **4 Computing efficiently** (the right pipes, power against the limit) -> **5 Memory bandwidth verdict** -> **6 Anomaly signals**.

- Stop at the first layer that answers "no". An unallocated GPU sitting idle is correct; there is nothing further down to diagnose.
- Sections 3-5 need the `DCGM_FI_PROF_*` profiling fields (Volta or newer, no concurrent Nsight/profiler session, and only one DCGM client watching them per node). Empty panels there mean the fields are not being collected, not that the GPU is idle.
- Section 1 job panels need the opt-in Slurm job exporter. Job-to-GPU attribution is node-level only: it reads as per-GPU truth only when the job owns the whole node.
- Thresholds and verdict boundaries on this page are heuristics, not measured limits.
- Fleet-wide view of the same layers: **Algalon / GPU Utilization Quality**.

panels.title: How to read this dashboard

panels.description:
Layer 1: is a job holding GPUs on this node? One row per Slurm job with a cgroup on the selected node, with the number of GPUs bound to it.

This is node-level on purpose. slurm-job-exporter labels each GPU with the index `nvidia-smi -L` prints inside the job's cgroup, which is not guaranteed to be the host-wide index dcgm-exporter uses for its `gpu` label, so this dashboard does not join a job to a specific DCGM GPU. On an exclusive node every GPU below belongs to the job listed here; on a shared node, use the per-job cgroup metrics in Algalon / Slurm Job Explorer instead.

Requires the opt-in slurm-job-exporter (job `slurm-job`, see docs/slurm.md) on this node; empty - not zero - without it.
panels.title: 1 Allocated: Slurm jobs holding GPUs on this node

panels.description:
GPUs on this node held by a Slurm job, next to the GPUs dcgm-exporter reports for it. Equal means the node is fully allocated, so any idle GPU further down is waste. Fewer bound than present means some GPUs are free, and idle readings on those are expected.

The "on node" count needs only DCGM. The "bound to jobs" count requires the opt-in slurm-job-exporter (job `slurm-job`, see docs/slurm.md) on this node; empty - not zero - without it.
panels.title: 1 Allocated: GPUs bound to jobs / on node

panels.description:
Selected GPUs holding less than 1 GiB of device memory. A job that has actually loaded a model or allocated its working set holds far more than that, so a non-zero count on a fully allocated node means a job holds the GPU without having put anything on it - still starting, failed during setup, or allocated more GPUs than it uses.

Needs only DCGM, so it is the device-side allocation check on clusters without the Slurm job exporter. The 1 GiB line is a heuristic.
panels.title: 1 Allocated: selected GPUs with < 1 GiB framebuffer used

panels.description: Device memory in use per GPU over time (DCGM reports MiB). A step up that then levels off is a job loading its model and working set. A line that keeps climbing is a leak or an unbounded cache inside the job; a drop to near zero while the job is still listed on the left means the process died and the allocation did not.
panels.title: 1 Allocated: framebuffer used per GPU

panels.description:
Layer 2: fraction of the sample during which a kernel was resident on the device. High is NOT efficiency - one active SM, or a kernel blocked on its input pipeline or an all-reduce, reads near 100%. Low on an allocated GPU is the allocated-idle pattern: the job holds the GPU and gives it nothing to do (SlurmJobGpuIdle pages on it per job).

If this is high, go to section 3 to see whether the resident kernel is actually computing.
panels.title: 2 Busy: GPU utilization per GPU

panels.description:
Selected GPUs whose utilization averaged under 5% over the last 30 minutes. Read it against section 1: on a node where jobs hold every GPU, each one counted here is allocated-idle - paid for and not used. On a node with free GPUs, idle is the expected state of the unallocated ones.

Find which GPU in the panel on the left. The 30-minute window matches the alert windows used elsewhere in Algalon; 5% is a heuristic.
panels.title: 2 Busy: idle GPUs (30m avg utilization < 5%)

panels.description:
Layer 3: are warps executing? SM active is the fraction of time at least one warp was running on an SM - the first signal that means work is actually happening. SM occupancy is how full the SMs were (resident warps against the hardware maximum); low occupancy with high SM active is small or register-heavy kernels. GR engine active is the coarsest of the three: the fraction of time the graphics/compute engine had any work at all.

SM active well under GPU utilization from section 2 means a resident kernel that is mostly waiting. Go to sections 4 and 5 to find out on what.

Requires the DCGM_FI_PROF_* profiling fields in monitoring/exporters/dcgm-counters.csv (Volta or newer; conflicts with a concurrent Nsight/profiler session). Empty without them.
panels.title: 3 Actually computing: SM active, SM occupancy, GR engine active

panels.description:
Per-GPU GPU utilization (scaled to 0-1) minus SM active - the busy-but-hollow gap for a single device. Near zero means "busy" is real computation. A wide, persistent positive gap means a kernel is resident while the SMs mostly sit idle: the bottleneck is the input pipeline, the CPU, storage or the interconnect, not the GPU. GpuBusyButHollow pages on the same condition at node level.

The subtraction matches the two series one-to-one per GPU: both come from the same dcgm-exporter with identical labelsets.

Requires the DCGM_FI_PROF_* profiling fields in monitoring/exporters/dcgm-counters.csv (Volta or newer; conflicts with a concurrent Nsight/profiler session). Empty without them.
panels.title: 3 Actually computing: busy minus SM active (hollow gap)

panels.description:
Layer 4: is the GPU computing on the units it was bought for? Fraction of cycles each arithmetic pipe was active. Matrix-heavy training and inference should be carried by the tensor pipe. Tensor low with FP32 high means the work is running as plain FP32 kernels - a missing mixed-precision setting or an op without a tensor-core path. FP64 is expected only for scientific codes. All pipes low with SM active high points at memory: go to section 5.

Requires the DCGM_FI_PROF_* profiling fields in monitoring/exporters/dcgm-counters.csv (Volta or newer; conflicts with a concurrent Nsight/profiler session). Empty without them.
panels.title: 4 Computing efficiently: pipe activity (tensor / FP16 / FP32 / FP64)

panels.description:
Fraction of cycles the device memory interface was sending or receiving data. High means the GPU is moving a lot of data through device memory - normal for memory-bound kernels, and the first input to the section 5 verdict, where it is read against tensor activity.

Requires the DCGM_FI_PROF_* profiling fields in monitoring/exporters/dcgm-counters.csv (Volta or newer; conflicts with a concurrent Nsight/profiler session). Empty without them.
panels.title: 4 Computing efficiently: DRAM active

panels.description: Power draw against the enforced power limit, per GPU. The layer-4 signal that needs no profiling fields: real training work sits around 0.7-1.0, while a GPU held at idle clocks inside an allocation sits at 0.1-0.3. A GPU that reads lower than its neighbours running the same job is either throttled (section 6) or doing less of the work.
panels.title: 4 Computing efficiently: power / enforced limit

panels.description:
Memory interface activity and tensor pipe activity of the same GPU on one axis. DRAM high and tensor low means the kernels are waiting on device memory bandwidth rather than computing - the memory-bound shape. Tensor high with DRAM moderate is the compute-bound case, where a training GPU should sit. Both low means the GPU is not being fed: go back to sections 1 and 2. The table below turns these combinations into a verdict.

Requires the DCGM_FI_PROF_* profiling fields in monitoring/exporters/dcgm-counters.csv (Volta or newer; conflicts with a concurrent Nsight/profiler session). Empty without them.
panels.title: 5 Memory bandwidth: DRAM active vs tensor active

panels.description:
Memory interface activity per unit of SM activity. SM active is clamped to a 0.01 floor so an idle GPU does not divide by zero. Around 1 or above, moving data is most of what the SMs spend their active time on; well below 1, the work is dominated by computation. Track how it moves for a given job rather than reading the absolute value - the boundary is a heuristic.

Requires the DCGM_FI_PROF_* profiling fields in monitoring/exporters/dcgm-counters.csv (Volta or newer; conflicts with a concurrent Nsight/profiler session). Empty without them.
panels.title: 5 Memory bandwidth: DRAM active / SM active

panels.description: Fraction of the sample during which device memory was being read or written, from the base (non-profiling) field set. Coarser than DRAM active and available on GPUs without DCP, so it is the fallback memory signal there. Where both exist and move in opposite directions, suspect the profiling sampler before the workload.
panels.title: 5 Memory bandwidth: memory copy utilization

panels.description:
Host-to-GPU traffic over PCIe, in bytes per second (DCGM reports these as rates, so they are plotted as-is). TX is GPU to host, RX is host to GPU. Low is normal for a training step that keeps its data on the device. Sustained high RX alongside low tensor activity means the GPU is waiting on host-side input copies or on offloaded memory (optimizer state, activations) being paged back.

Requires the DCGM_FI_PROF_* profiling fields in monitoring/exporters/dcgm-counters.csv (Volta or newer; conflicts with a concurrent Nsight/profiler session). Empty without them.
panels.title: 5 Memory bandwidth: PCIe TX / RX

panels.description:
GPU-to-GPU traffic over NVLink, in bytes per second summed over all links of the GPU (DCGM reports these as rates). Tensor- and expert-parallel collectives drive it. High NVLink traffic with low tensor activity points at communication, not memory bandwidth, as the wait: compare with the NVLink error panel in section 6, since retransmissions slow collectives without showing up in GPU utilization.

Requires the DCGM_FI_PROF_* profiling fields in monitoring/exporters/dcgm-counters.csv (Volta or newer; conflicts with a concurrent Nsight/profiler session). Empty without them.
panels.title: 5 Memory bandwidth: NVLink TX / RX

panels.description: Combines the section 3-5 panels into a verdict on whether memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. "Waiting" sends you to Node Health; "not fed" sends you back to sections 1 and 2.

options.content:
| What the panels show | Verdict | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| DRAM active near its ceiling, tensor low, SM occupancy high | **Memory-bandwidth bound** | Larger batches, operator fusion, lower-precision weights or activations |
| DRAM low, SM active low, GPU utilization high | **Waiting** - on CPU, storage or the input pipeline | Algalon / Host Saturation (USE) for this node (CPU, memory, IO), then Algalon / Node Health for NFS latency |
| High NVLink or PCIe traffic, tensor low, DRAM moderate | **Communication bound** | Section 6 NVLink errors, then the parallelism strategy of the job |
| Everything low | **Not fed** - no work arriving | Sections 1 and 2: is a job allocated, is it running? |
| Tensor high, DRAM moderate | **Compute bound** - healthy | Nothing to fix |

These boundaries are heuristics, not measured limits. All of them need the `DCGM_FI_PROF_*` profiling fields; without those, power against the enforced limit (section 4) and memory copy utilization are the only signals left.

panels.title: 5 Memory bandwidth: how to read the verdict

panels.description:
XID errors dcgm-exporter observed on each GPU within its counting window (5 minutes by default), split by XID code. Non-zero for a code means the driver reported that fault on this GPU during the window.

XID is a post-mortem signal: by the time it appears the GPU has already stopped doing useful work, and anything on the panels above around that time is the aftermath. Look up the code in NVIDIA's XID catalogue; Algalon treats 31/43/94 as warning (application restart), 119/145/149 as critical (GPU reset) and 79 as critical (node reboot). Early warning comes from the node_exporter precursor rules on Node Health, not from here.
panels.title: 6 Anomalies: XID errors (5m window, by code)

panels.description: Fraction of wall time each GPU spent clock-limited by its power cap or by temperature. DCGM reports cumulative violation time in nanoseconds, so the per-second rate divided by 1e9 is the throttled share of time. Any sustained non-zero value means the clocks are being held down and the same work takes longer: power points at the power limit or facility capping, thermal at cooling.
panels.title: 6 Anomalies: power / thermal throttle time

panels.description: NVLink CRC (flit and data), replay and recovery errors added in the last 5 minutes, per GPU. Zero is normal. Increases mean the link is retransmitting: collectives slow down while GPU utilization stays unchanged, which is why this belongs next to the efficiency panels. Recovery errors are the most serious of the four. Check the cabling or NVSwitch path, the GPU baseboard and the driver log for the node.
panels.title: 6 Anomalies: NVLink errors (5m increase)

panels.description: SM clock per GPU. Under load it should sit near the GPU's boost clock and match its neighbours. A GPU running lower than its peers under the same job is being braked - read it with the throttle panel above and DCGM_FI_DEV_CLOCKS_EVENT_REASONS on Node Health. Low clocks while idle are normal.
panels.title: 6 Anomalies: SM clock
